title: Which universal is this? Categories, constituents, sentence types, hierarchy and recursion
summary: From zero: what each of the five properties every human language shares actually means, what it looks like in a real sentence, and how to name the property from one example in a few seconds.
sourceNote: Week 1 handout 'Introduction' (Dr. Nie), the Aug 20 lecture, and Carnie, Syntax ch. 1. The examples are the handout's (the cat in the hat, the thief with a cane, the Times reported that Sarah won) plus classic textbook ones. Later weeks go deeper on each: categories (Week 2), constituents (Weeks 4 to 5), trees (Week 6).

sections.heading: The big picture in one minute

blocks.md: A **universal** is a property that every human language has. Not most languages: all of them, from English to Arabic to sign languages. Dr. Nie's Week 1 handout lists five, and the question you'll keep hearing is *Which universal is this?*: you get one example and you name the property it shows.

Think of a sentence like a Lego build. **Categories** are the kinds of bricks. **Constituents** are bricks snapped into pieces. **Sentence types** are the finished shapes (a statement, a question, a command). **Hierarchy** says pieces go *inside* pieces, and where they snap changes the meaning. **Recursion** says a piece can hold a piece of the same kind, forever.

blocks.caption: The five universals, smallest idea to biggest. The question under each is the one to ask yourself when you see an example.

blocks.md: **Why it matters** Every other week of this class zooms in on one of these five. Categories become Week 2, constituents become Weeks 4 and 5, hierarchy becomes the trees of Week 6. If the five are clear now, every later chapter is just detail. And on the oral exam, 'which property does this show, and how do you know?' is the easiest points you can bank.
blocks.label: why

blocks.body: A group of words that can go in the **same slots** in a sentence and take the **same endings**. Noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, determiner and so on. (You may know them as parts of speech.)

blocks.md: **One example.** Take the frame *The ___ slept.* The words that fit the hole are nouns: *dog*, *baby*, even *idea*. The words that don't fit are not nouns: 'The happy slept' and 'The quickly slept' are broken. The hole is doing the sorting, not the meaning.

blocks.title: The main categories and a frame for each

blocks.body: Don't define a category by meaning. *Destruction* is an action but it's a noun (*the destruction*, *destructions*). *Happiness* is a feeling but it's a noun. Dr. Nie wants a **test**: 'it fits after *the* and takes plural *-s*, so it's a noun.'
blocks.slide: Trap: meaning is not the test

blocks.md: **How you'll recognize it in an example:** the example is about **one word** (or a few words) and **which slot they fit or which ending they take**. If you see a frame with a blank, or a list of words that 'pattern together', answer *categories*.

blocks.prompt: *Every*, *the*, *this* and *his* can all fill the blank in '___ dog barked.' Which universal does this show?
blocks.answer: **Categories.** The four words share a slot, so they share a category (they're all determiners).

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this** Your phone's autocorrect and every grammar checker start by tagging each word with a category (this step is called part-of-speech tagging, and LING 115 builds one). 'Time flies like an arrow' confuses them because *flies* and *like* can each be in two categories.
blocks.label: world

sections.heading: Constituents: words team up into units

blocks.body: A group of words that acts as **one single unit** in a sentence. You prove it with a test: can you **replace** it with one word, **move** it as a block, or use it **alone as an answer**?

blocks.md: **One example.** In *The cat in the hat sat on the mat*, the words *in the hat* are a unit. Ask *Where was the cat?* and you can answer *In the hat.* But *hat sat* is not a unit, even though the two words sit side by side. No question has *hat sat* as its answer.

blocks.title: Running the three tests on 'the evidence'

lines: The spies will stash [the evidence] after midnight.
frames.caption: Is *the evidence* one unit? Three tests. Passing any one is enough.

lines: The spies will stash [the evidence] after midnight.
The spies will stash [it] after midnight.  ✓
frames.caption: Test 1, replace: one pronoun, *it*, swaps out both words. ✓

lines: The spies will stash [the evidence] after midnight.
The spies will stash [it] after midnight.  ✓
[The evidence], the spies will stash after midnight.  ✓
frames.caption: Test 2, move: the two words move to the front together and the sentence still works. ✓

lines: The spies will stash [the evidence] after midnight.
The spies will stash [it] after midnight.  ✓
[The evidence], the spies will stash after midnight.  ✓
What will the spies stash? [The evidence.]  ✓
frames.caption: Test 3, answer: it can stand alone as the answer to a question. ✓ So *the evidence* is a constituent.

lines: Now try [stash the]:
*The spies will [it] evidence.  ✗
*[Stash the], the spies will evidence.  ✗
What will the spies do? *[Stash the.]  ✗
frames.caption: Same tests on *stash the*: every one fails. Not a unit, even though the words are neighbors.

blocks.caption: The cat in the hat, as a tree. Every node is a constituent. Click **PP** over *in the hat*: it's one unit. Now look for a single node covering just *hat sat*: there isn't one, and that's why it fails the tests.

params.bracket: [TP [DP [D The] [NP [N cat] [PP [P in] [DP [D the] [NP [N hat]]]]]] [T PAST] [VP [V sat] [PP [P on] [DP [D the] [NP [N mat]]]]]]

blocks.body: A constituent can be one word or many words. And a unit is decided by **tests**, not by 'it sounds like it goes together'. Always name the test you used.

blocks.md: **How you'll recognize it in an example:** the example **replaces, moves, or isolates a chunk of words** (*in the hat → there*, *the evidence* fronted, a one-phrase answer). If a group of words is being treated as one piece, answer *constituents*.

blocks.prompt: 'Put the book **on the shelf**.' → 'Put the book **there**.' Which universal?
blocks.answer: **Constituents.** One word (*there*) replaced three, so *on the shelf* is one unit.

blocks.body: The overall **shape** a sentence is built in, which matches the job it does. Every language has at least three: **declarative** (a statement), **interrogative** (a question), and **imperative** (a command).

blocks.md: **One example.** Same ingredients, three shapes: *The dog is quiet.* (declarative) · *Is the dog quiet?* (interrogative) · *Be quiet!* (imperative). The words barely change, but the arrangement tells you whether you're stating, asking, or ordering.

cards.title: Declarative
lines: Makes a claim that can be true or false.
Shape: subject, then verb.
*Sarah won the race.*

cards.title: Interrogative: yes/no
lines: Asks for yes or no.
English: the helper verb jumps before the subject.
*Did Sarah win the race?*

cards.title: Interrogative: wh-
lines: Asks for information.
Starts with who, what, where, when, why, how.
*What did Sarah win?*

cards.title: Imperative
lines: Tells someone to do something.
No spoken subject: the 'you' is understood.
*Win the race!*

data.note: A fourth type, the exclamative (*What a race that was!*), shows up in many languages too.

blocks.caption: The sentence types. Two kinds of question, because a yes/no question and a wh-question are built differently.

blocks.md: **Other languages build them differently, but they all have them.** Arabic makes a yes/no question by adding the particle *hal* at the front: *hal qaraʔta l-kitāb?* 'Did you read the book?'. Japanese adds *ka* at the end. English moves a helper verb. Different tools, same universal: every language has a way to ask.

blocks.body: The type is about **shape**, not punctuation or tone. *Could you pass the salt?* has question shape (interrogative) even though it's really a polite request. On the exam, name the shape and, if you want extra credit, say the job it's doing.

blocks.md: **How you'll recognize it in an example:** the example compares **whole sentences** as statement vs question vs command, or asks you to name one. If the whole sentence's shape is the point, answer *sentence types*.

blocks.prompt: 'Sit down.' / 'Are you sitting?' / 'You are sitting.' Which universal do these three show together?
blocks.answer: **Sentence types.** One imperative, one interrogative, one declarative.

sections.heading: Hierarchy: units inside units, and grouping decides meaning

blocks.body: Constituents sit **inside** bigger constituents, like boxes in boxes. The **grouping**, not just the left-to-right order, decides what a sentence means and how rules apply to it.

blocks.md: **One example.** *The thief tripped the man with a cane.* Who has the cane? It depends on the grouping. If *with a cane* groups with *tripped*, the thief used the cane. If it groups with *the man*, the man was holding it. The word order is identical, so only the **structure** can tell the two apart.

blocks.md: **The second kind of evidence: rules follow structure, not counting.** To turn *The man who is tall is happy* into a question, you move an *is* to the front. But which one? If English counted words and moved the first *is*, you'd get nonsense. Every speaker moves the *is* of the **main** clause and skips the one tucked inside the subject. Nobody teaches kids this. The rule 'sees' the boxes.

blocks.body: Constituents vs hierarchy: **constituents** is 'this group is one unit' (one box). **Hierarchy** is 'boxes sit inside boxes, and *which* box something is in matters' (the nesting and its effect). If the example shows **two meanings from one order**, or a rule that must see structure, it's hierarchy.
blocks.slide: Trap: one box vs boxes in boxes

blocks.md: **How you'll recognize it in an example:** look for **one word order with two meanings** (an attachment ambiguity) or a **rule that ignores the linear order** and follows the structure. Answer *hierarchy*.

blocks.prompt: 'I saw the girl with the telescope.' Which universal explains why it has two meanings?
blocks.answer: **Hierarchy.** *with the telescope* can group with *saw* (I used the telescope) or with *the girl* (she had it). Same order, different grouping.

sections.heading: Recursion: a unit inside a unit of the same kind, forever

blocks.body: A unit can contain **another unit of the same type**, and that one can contain another, with **no upper limit**. A clause inside a clause, a noun phrase inside a noun phrase. It's why there is no longest sentence.

blocks.md: **One example.** *I remember that John told me that the Times reported that Sarah won.* Each *that*-clause holds another *that*-clause. You could always add *that her coach said that…*. The grammar never runs out, even though your breath does.

blocks.title: Growing a sentence one clause at a time

lines: Sarah won.
frames.caption: Start with one clause. A clause is a subject plus a verb.

lines: Sarah won.
the Times reported [that Sarah won].
frames.caption: Wrap it: the whole old clause becomes a piece INSIDE a new clause. Clause inside clause.

lines: Sarah won.
the Times reported [that Sarah won].
John told me [that the Times reported [that Sarah won]].
frames.caption: Wrap again. Same move, same type of box.

lines: Sarah won.
the Times reported [that Sarah won].
John told me [that the Times reported [that Sarah won]].
I remember [that John told me [that the Times reported [that Sarah won]]].
frames.caption: And again. Four clauses, three of them nested. The rule that builds it is one rule used over and over.

lines: I remember [that John told me [that the Times reported [that Sarah won]]].
…and you could wrap it again, and again, forever.
frames.caption: That's recursion: no rule says 'stop at four'. That's why a language has infinitely many sentences built from a finite set of words and rules.

blocks.body: **Long is not recursive.** *big red shiny ball* has three adjectives, but no unit sits inside a unit of the same type the way a clause holds a clause. And *hierarchy* vs *recursion*: every recursive example is hierarchical, but recursion is the special case where the **same type** repeats inside itself. If you can point to 'a clause inside a clause' (or NP in NP), say recursion.

blocks.md: **How you'll recognize it in an example:** the example has **the same structure repeated inside itself** (*that… that… that…*, *'s … 's … 's*, *of the… of the…*), and you can imagine adding one more. Answer *recursion*.

blocks.prompt: 'the dog that chased the cat that ate the mouse' Which universal?
blocks.answer: **Recursion.** A relative clause (*that ate the mouse*) sits inside another relative clause (*that chased the cat…*).

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this** Recursion is exactly how programming languages work: an *if* inside an *if*, a function that calls itself (CS 146), brackets inside brackets. The grammars that compilers use to read code came straight out of this idea in linguistics.
blocks.label: world

sections.heading: Which universal is this? The five-question method

blocks.md: When you get an example, don't guess. Ask these five questions **in order** and stop at the first *yes*. The order goes from smallest idea (one word) to biggest (endless nesting), so the easy ones catch first.

rows: Is it about **which slot a word fits** or which ending it takes?
a frame with a blank; 'these words pattern together'; noun / verb / adjective
Is a **group of words acting as one piece** (replaced, moved, or used as an answer)?
→ it / there / do so; a phrase moved to the front; a short answer
Is it about the **shape of the whole sentence**: statement, question, command?
a period vs a question vs an order; *hal*, *ka*, moving *did*
Does **the same word order have two meanings**, or does a rule **skip over structure**?
'with a cane', 'with the telescope', 'old men and women', 'Is the man who is tall happy?'
Is a unit **inside a unit of the same type**, and could it **go on forever**?
that… that… that…; 's… 's…; of the… of the…
blocks.title: The five questions
Worked example 1
blocks.body: 'The students **who finished early** left.' → 'The students left.' Which universal is shown by the bold part coming out as a block?
blocks.answer: **Constituents.** The bold words were removed together and the rest still works, so they act as one unit. (If the question were about *who finished early* sitting inside the subject and making a rule skip it, that would be hierarchy.)

blocks.title: Worked example 2
blocks.body: 'Visiting relatives can be boring.' Are the relatives visiting you, or are you visiting them?
blocks.answer: **Hierarchy.** One word order, two groupings: [visiting relatives] as people who visit, or [visiting] [relatives] as an activity. Two structures, two meanings.

blocks.title: Worked example 3
blocks.body: 'She said that he thinks that they know.'
blocks.answer: **Recursion.** A *that*-clause inside a *that*-clause inside the main clause. Same type in same type, and you could add more.

blocks.title: Worked example 4
blocks.answer: **Categories.** The slot sorts the words: the first three are verbs, the others nouns.

blocks.title: Worked example 5
blocks.body: English 'Did you eat?', Arabic 'hal akalta?', Japanese 'Tabemashita ka?'
blocks.answer: **Sentence types.** Three languages, three different tools, but every one has a yes/no question shape. That's the universal.

blocks.answer: **Recursion.** A possessor (*the teacher's*) sits inside a possessor (*the teacher's student's*). Same type in same type.

rows: A property every human language has.
A kind of word defined by the slots it fits and the endings it takes (noun, verb…).
A group of words that acts as one unit; proven by replace, move, or answer tests.
The shape of a whole sentence: declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command).
Units inside units; the grouping decides meaning and how rules apply.
A unit inside a unit of the same type, with no limit.
One word order, two groupings, two meanings (the cane sentence).
A short word that replaces a whole unit: it, there, do so.
